QF.id: AIFM CIII Modern Portfolio Theory and Capital Market Theory_20

question.text: Mr. Vivek Joshi tells his team that portfolios lying to the RIGHT of the market portfolio 'M' on the Capital Market Line represent borrowing at the risk-free rate and investing in the market portfolio. For Himalaya Arbitrage Fund (Cat III AIF) operating under SEBI constraints, what is the MOST important manager-side caveat?

answer.text: Cat III AIFs cannot borrow at all, so the right-of-M region is theoretically inaccessible.

Cat III AIFs face a 2x leverage cap (total exposure, after permitted offsetting, not to exceed 2x of NAV), so the CML can be traversed to the right only up to that limit and at a borrowing rate above Rf.
Cat III AIFs can borrow only from the sponsor, limiting leverage to sponsor commitment.
The CML is irrelevant for Cat III AIFs because they use derivatives, not leverage.

explanation.text: The Logic: Capital Market Theory allows risk-free borrowing to scale returns beyond M on the CML (workbook page 58). For a Cat III AIF, SEBI (AIF) Regulations impose a 2x leverage cap: total exposure after permitted offsetting shall not exceed twice the NAV (pages 409-410). In practice, the right-of-M region is accessible only within this cap, and actual borrowing rates exceed the theoretical Rf because practical financing is above the risk-free lending rate. The Trap: (A) is incorrect — Cat I/II AIFs are zero-leverage; Cat III is NOT. (C) invents a restriction that doesn't exist in the regulations. (D) wrongly separates derivatives from leverage — derivatives do create exposure that counts toward the cap. Note: Workbook pages 58 and 62-64 cover the CML and risk-free asset; pages 409-410 cover the Cat III leverage limit and breach-reporting requirement. Use the workbook phrasing "total exposure after permitted offsetting" rather than informal "gross exposure".
